newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives may face bitter leadership scrap.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives may face bitter leadership scrap.

text.p: With polls indicating voters will cast Britain's Conservatives into the political desert on Thursday, speculation is now centred on the election after the election -- the one for the Conservative party's leadership.
How a party that was deeply and openly divided even in office would react to the reality of opposition after 18 years in power is fascinating political analysts.
Their conclusion -- it would not be a pretty sight if Prime Minister John Major resigns quickly and leaves a number of former ministers to fight tooth and nail for the party's ideological soul.

"It would be an extremely bloody affair," said Ivor Crewe, professor of government at the University of Essex. "There would be two civil wars going on -- between right and left and within these two camps."
Analysts said it would help the Conservative Party if Major stayed on until the annual leadership election in the autumn rather than resign immediately as Labour leader Neil Kinnock did in 1992.

Philip Norton, professor of government at the University of Hull, said much would depend on the size of any Conservative defeat and the level of agitation in the parliamentary party, particularly from Euro-sceptics who have sniped at Major for the past four years.

"It would probably be in the party's benefit to stand back and take stock. It would not be in the candidates' benefit to go for an early (leadership) election as they would not have time to build up their support and become front-runners," he said.

Much could depend on the scale of any defeat. Polling expert Peter Kellner predicts the party could win just 210 of the 659 seats at stake, less than two thirds of the number they won in the 1992 election, if opinion polls are right.

Such an electoral earthquake could leave some ministers and possible future candidates, such as Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, without a parliamentary seat. But there would still be at least five candidates for Major's job from both wings of the party, none of whom can be considered favourite.

Right-wingers such as Defence Secretary Michael Portillo and John Redwood, the former cabinet minister who unsuccessfully challenged Major for the leadership in 1995, are expected to press for an early poll. Representing the centre of the party would be Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine and possibly Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell. The "left" of the party would look to finance minister and pro-European Kenneth Clarke.
But most of these ministers have powerful enemies as well as vocal supporters. "There are so few unifiers who have broad support," said Norton. "The only obvious unity card is the incumbent (Major)".

The wild card, and strongly fancied by bookmakers, is Welsh Secretary William Hague. Only 36, Hague has not been in government long enough to make enemies and has been careful to keep equi-distant between the pro- and anti-Europeans. Another possible successor, and probably Major's choice, is Chris Patten. He is currently out of the running, having lost his seat at the last election in 1992 and gone off to Hong Kong as the colony's last British governor.
But his job there ends on June 30 and he could theoretically be back in parliament in time for any autumn leadership battle.
Analysts say if the Conservatives vote in a candidate from the right of the party, a split cannot be ruled out.
"You might get 10 or 20 Conservative MPs, for a mixture of little Englander and personal motives, quitting," said Tom Nossiter, politics lecturer at the London School of Economics.
Crewe said Labour might even try to court Conservative left-wingers if a right-winger won the leadership.
